{{Short description|American physicist}}

'''Norman Myles Kroll''' (6 April 1922, [[Tulsa, Oklahoma]] – 8 August 2004, [[La Jolla, California]]) was an American theoretical physicist, known for his pioneering work in [[Quantum electrodynamics|QED]].<ref name=PhysicsTodayObit>{{cite journal|author=Goldberger, Marvin|authorlink=Marvin Leonard Goldberger|author2=Kuti, Julius|title=Obituary. Norman Myles Kroll|journal=Physics Today|date=December 2004|volume=58|issue=12|page=82|doi=10.1063/1.2169457|bibcode = 2005PhT....58l..82G |doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Life ==
Kroll received in 1942 his bachelor's degree from [[Columbia University]] after 2 years of study, having studied from 1938 to 1940 at [[Rice University]] in [[Houston]]. During WW II he did theoretical radar research ([[magnetron]] theory),<ref>{{cite book|author=Schweber, Silvan S.|chapter=3.4 Training a New Generation of Physicists: Norman Kroll|title=QED and the men who made it: Dyson, Feynman, Schwinger, and Tomonaga|publisher=Princeton University Press|year=1994|pages=141–144|isbn=0691033277|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=61n5dE7FJQgC&pg=PA141}}</ref> during 1943–1945,<ref name=ACAP>{{Cite web |url=https://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?krolln |title=Norman Kroll {{!}} Array of Contemporary American Physicists |access-date=2016-04-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160307143455/https://www.aip.org/history/acap/biographies/bio.jsp?krolln |archive-date=2016-03-07 |url-status=dead }}</ref> at Columbia under the supervision of [[Willis Lamb]] and [[Isidor Isaac Rabi|I. I. Rabi]]. In 1943 Kroll received his master's degree and in 1948 his PhD from Columbia University with Lamb as thesis advisor.
 
{{blockquote|He collaborated with Lamb on their famous paper "On the Self-Energy of a Bound Electron," which was published in 1949 in the ''Physical Review'' and reprinted by Dover Publications in 1959 as part of ''Selected Papers on Quantum Electrodynamics''. Based on Kroll's thesis work, the paper provided the first theoretical explanation of the [[Lamb shift]] in QED and became one of the most important landmarks of the field.<ref name=PhysicsTodayObit/>}}

In the academic year 1948–1949 he was a visiting scholar at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]], where he, with [[Robert Karplus]], calculated the QED two-loop contributions for the [[Landé factor|anomalous magnetic moment]] of the electron.<ref>{{cite book|author=Kaiser, David|authorlink=David Kaiser (physicist)|chapter=Kroll's Perturbative Bookkeepers|pages=209–220|title=Drawing theories apart: The dispersion of Feynman diagrams in postwar physics|publisher=University of Chicago Press|year=2009|isbn=9780226422657|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_wz9JZvBt78C&pg=PA209}}</ref> Kroll was, with Lamb, one of the first (including [[Victor Weisskopf]] and his student [[James Bruce French|Bruce French]]) to calculate the relativistic Lamb shift (after [[Hans Bethe]] made a rough, non-relativistic estimate for it).<ref>{{cite book|author=Mehra, Jagdish|authorlink=Jagdish Mehra|title=The Conceptual Completion and Extensions of Quantum Mechanics 1932-1941. Epilogue: Aspects of the Further Development of Quantum Theory 1942-1999: Subject Index: Volumes 1 to 6|pages=1040–1042|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|year=2004|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6jTaBwAAQBAJ&pg=PA104|isbn=9780387218052}}</ref> This work was part of the pioneering efforts that led to the QED formalism developed by [[Richard Feynman]], [[Julian Schwinger]], and [[Sin-Itiro Tomonaga]].

Kroll became at Columbia an assistant professor in 1949 and was promoted to associate professor and then full professor before leaving for [[University of California, San Diego|UCSD]].

{{blockquote|In 1962, UCSD recruited Kroll to become one of its physics department's founding members and thereby bring to UCSD the prestige and recognition of a world leader in research. During his four decades at UCSD, Kroll continued his research in QED, developed with [[Marshall Rosenbluth]] a theory of the free electron laser, and participated in the design of particle accelerators. In addition, he made numerous contributions to the development of UCSD as one of the nation's leading research universities and twice served as chair of UCSD's physics department, from 1963 to 1965 and from 1983 to 1988.<ref name=PhysicsTodayObit/>}}

In 1960–1981 he was a member of the [[JASON Defense Advisory Group]].<ref name="ACAP" />

Among his doctoral students are [[Robert Mills (physicist)|Robert Mills]] and [[Eyvind Wichmann]].<ref name="NASbio">{{cite journal |author=Kroll, Joseph |author2=Kuti, Julius |author3=Ruderman, Malvin |year=2015 |title=Norman M. Kroll 1922–2004 |url=https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/kroll-norman.pdf |journal=Biographical Memoirs of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=2015 |page=1 |bibcode=2015BMNAS2015....1K}}</ref>

Upon his death, Kroll was survived by his wife, four children, and nine grandchildren.<ref name="NASbio" />

== Honors ==
In the academic year 1955–1956 he was a Sloan Fellow and a Guggenheim Fellow at the University of Rome. He was elected in 1974 to the [[National Academy of Sciences]]. He was a Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] and a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]].<ref name="ACAP" />
